title: Joint Symmetry And Dynamical Accessibility In Compact Hamiltonian Encodings Of Set Cover
authors: Fabricio de Souza Luiz
abstract: ArXiv:2608.11503v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Which part of a Hamiltonian spectrum is physically relevant when both the initial state and interpolation preserve several symmetries? We address this question for a compact multi-register encoding of Minimum Set Cover. The represented symmetry combines register permutations with the faithful base action of the incidence automorphism group. We distinguish its fixed, symmetry-allowed space from the generally smaller cyclic space generated by the protocol and define gaps relative to isolated bands in that space. A sector-resolved Schur-complement bound certifies cover-measurement probability whenever the sector contains feasible covers and has positive invalid-state separation; the sector kinetic floor is essential. Exact orbit quotients expose inter-sector coincidences invisible to a symmetric protocol, while a stability theorem shows that transverse dark crossings persist under small symmetry-preserving perturbations. On an even-cycle family, the original linear interpolation has an exact global multiplicity closure while the joint-fixed excitation gap remains constant. For the same family we construct a Johnson/Metropolis parent path from a Dicke state to a Gibbs-amplitude state with cover probability [MATH]. A zero-range comparison and a log-concave three-box coupling give the uniform cyclic-gap certificate [MATH]. Quantitative derivative bounds then yield a polynomial adiabatic runtime in the abstract Hamiltonian-access model, conditional on Dicke-state preparation and access to the parent Hamiltonian. We make no quantum-speedup claim: the result is a rigorous separation of global, symmetry-allowed, and dynamically accessible spectral structure. Changing the initial state or breaking a preserved symmetry changes that accessible spectrum.
tldr: This paper analyzes the spectral structure of a Hamiltonian encoding for Minimum Set Cover, distinguishing symmetry-allowed and dynamically accessible subspaces, and provides rigorous bounds on adiabatic runtime.
motivation: The work aims to understand which parts of a Hamiltonian spectrum are physically relevant when symmetries are preserved, and to characterize the gap between symmetry-allowed and dynamically accessible spaces in a quantum optimization context.
method: The authors use a compact multi-register encoding of Minimum Set Cover, apply representation theory to decompose the Hilbert space, and derive sector-resolved Schur-complement bounds and stability theorems. They also construct a Johnson/Metropolis parent path and use zero-range and log-concave couplings to certify gaps.
result: They prove a polynomial adiabatic runtime in the abstract Hamiltonian-access model, conditional on Dicke-state preparation, and show that transverse dark crossings persist under small symmetry-preserving perturbations. They also demonstrate exact global multiplicity closure for even-cycle families.

title: Exact Dynamics Of First-order System-bath Coherence In Bilinear Bosonic Models
authors: Yang-Yang Xie, Song-Lin Wu, Paul Brumer, Zhao-Ming Wang, Lian-Ao Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2608.11556v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the exact dynamics of first-order system--bath coherence induced by excitation exchange in bilinear bosonic models. By solving the linear Heisenberg equations, we obtain the exact evolution of system and bath operators and evaluate the first-order coherence between the system mode and the collective bath mode directly coupled to it. We analyze how this coherence depends on initial occupations, coupling strength, spectral width, and detuning, showing that its buildup and oscillatory behavior are closely related to excitation exchange and reservoir memory. We further examine controlled coherence dynamics under leakage-elimination-operator inspired modulation of the system frequency. The results show that random modulation can suppress excitation leakage and maintain finite and relatively stable coherence fluctuations at long times. These results clarify the evolution and control of first-order system--bath coherence in settings where a localized bosonic mode is coupled to a structured bosonic reservoir.

They also study controlled dynamics under leakage-elimination-operator inspired modulation.

title: Efficient Quantum Modular Reduction: Crandall Reduction And Its Fault-tolerant Resource Analysis
authors: Changyeol Lee, Sungyeon Kook, Wooyeong Song, Kwangil Bae, Wonhyuk Lee, Ilkwon Sohn
abstract: ArXiv:2608.11563v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modular arithmetic is central to quantum algorithms for cryptographic problems, including Shor's algorithm and Grover-based cryptanalysis, with modular reduction contributing substantially to circuit cost. Pseudo-Mersenne moduli [MATH] allow classical Crandall reduction to replace division with folding and constant arithmetic, providing a structural opportunity for more efficient quantum modular reduction than Barrett reduction. We translate this advantage into a reversible quantum setting by deriving explicit folding and normalization conditions for [MATH]-bit inputs. To the best of our knowledge, this constitutes the first exact reversible quantum circuit formulation of Crandall reduction. Based on this formulation, we develop two variants: Crandall reduction-1 is designed to minimize execution cost through one-step normalization, whereas Crandall reduction-2 uses two-step normalization to support a wider range of [MATH] with limited overhead. Logical resource estimates show that both variants require fewer qubits and lower T-count and T-depth than optimized folding Barrett reduction. At [MATH], Crandall reduction-1 reduces both T-count and T-depth by approximately 46.9% relative to optimized folding Barrett reduction. Surface-code analysis further shows that, at [MATH] under the Sparse Blossom decoder, the estimated runtimes of the two variants are 30.05 ms and 35.39 ms, respectively, compared with 53.77 ms for optimized folding Barrett reduction. These results demonstrate the practical value of exploiting modulus-specific arithmetic structure in fault-tolerant quantum circuit design.
tldr: This paper presents the first reversible quantum circuit formulation of Crandall reduction for modular arithmetic, achieving significant resource savings over Barrett reduction in fault-tolerant quantum circuits.
motivation: Modular reduction is a major cost in quantum algorithms for cryptography, and exploiting modulus-specific structure like pseudo-Mersenne moduli can lead to more efficient circuits.
method: The authors derive explicit folding and normalization conditions for Crandall reduction in a reversible quantum setting, and develop two variants (one-step and two-step normalization) with logical resource estimates and surface-code analysis.
result: Both variants require fewer qubits and lower T-count and T-depth than optimized folding Barrett reduction, with up to ~46.9% reduction in T-count and T-depth at n=2048, and faster estimated runtimes under surface-code decoding.
conclusion: Exploiting modulus-specific arithmetic structure can significantly improve the efficiency of quantum modular reduction, which is valuable for fault-tolerant quantum implementations of cryptographic algorithms.

title: Efficient Compilation For Hamiltonian Simulation Via Global Binary Symplectic Form Simplification
authors: Zhaohui Yang, Yuwei Han, Ruiyun Zhang, Dawei Ding, Jianxin Chen, Yuan Feng, Yuan Xie
abstract: ArXiv:2608.11579v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hamiltonian simulation is a core quantum workload, underpinning variational quantum algorithms and Trotterized time evolution. Such programs are expressed as Pauli exponential sequences, exhibiting structural patterns that are highly amenable to high-level synthesis and optimization. Existing compilers, however, fail to fully unlock the optimization potential of their global algebraic structure, even when employing advanced graph- or tableau-based methods. We present Symphony, a holistic compilation approach built on the binary symplectic form (BSF) representation of Pauli strings. Unlike prior group-wise BSF simplification and path-based Pauli network synthesis, Symphony applies generalized controlled-Pauli Clifford transformations directly to a global BSF tableau, adaptively reducing active Pauli rows and emitting eligible two-qubit blocks other than single-qubit rotations in a forward Clifford frame. Following algebraic simplification, Symphony performs a causality-preserving block rescheduling heuristic that respects frame-induced dependencies while exposing extensive two-qubit block parallelism opportunities. This streamlined compilation style comprehensively exploits simultaneous simplification and commutativity opportunities, achieving efficient global optimization without relying on computationally expensive heuristics or long-horizon searches. Across the generic Hamiltonian simulation benchmarks in HamLib, Symphony achieves average reductions of 59% in two-qubit gate count and 91% in circuit depth. It strictly Pareto-dominates prior state-of-the-art compilers, requiring 1.14--1.58[MATH] fewer two-qubit gates and especially shrinking two-qubit circuit depth by a substantial factor of 1.87--5.67[MATH] on average.
tldr: This paper presents Symphony, a compiler for Hamiltonian simulation that uses global binary symplectic form simplification to significantly reduce two-qubit gate count and circuit depth.
motivation: Hamiltonian simulation is a core quantum workload, but existing compilers fail to fully exploit the global algebraic structure of Pauli exponential sequences, leaving optimization potential untapped.
method: Symphony applies generalized controlled-Pauli Clifford transformations to a global BSF tableau, adaptively reducing active Pauli rows and emitting two-qubit blocks in a forward Clifford frame, followed by a causality-preserving block rescheduling heuristic.
result: On HamLib benchmarks, Symphony achieves average reductions of 59% in two-qubit gate count and 91% in circuit depth, strictly Pareto-dominating prior state-of-the-art compilers.
conclusion: The proposed compilation approach demonstrates that global algebraic simplification can yield substantial improvements in Hamiltonian simulation circuits, offering a practical tool for quantum computing.

title: Quantum Channel-Induced Geometry Of The Uhlmann Phase In Qubit Systems
authors: F. Nieto-Guadarrama, F. Rojas, J. Villavicencio, Jes\'us A. Maytorena
abstract: ArXiv:2608.11714v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that a cyclically controlled non-coherence-generating channel supplies a two-parameter family of closed Bloch trajectories, absent in the single-parameter (temperature) cycles of the thermal Uhlmann literature, whose associated Uhlmann phase develops a genuine vortex--antivortex structure on the channel-parameter torus. A qubit prepared in a pure state, which carries no geometric phase of its own, acquires a nontrivial Uhlmann phase, obtained here in closed form, purely from a closed loop in the space of the native quantum channel parameters. The net topological charge of these defects is constrained to zero by the Poincar\'e--Hopf theorem. As the input-state orientation approaches its critical values, the defects merge and annihilate in pairs following a square-root coalescence law. This defect dynamics drives local geometric transitions, a mechanism that contrasts with single-parameter thermal Uhlmann transitions, where a global quantized winding jumps as a bulk invariant.

motivation: To extend the study of geometric phases in mixed-state quantum systems beyond single-parameter thermal cycles, exploring the role of channel parameters in generating nontrivial Uhlmann phases.
method: The authors consider a cyclically controlled non-coherence-generating channel acting on a qubit, derive the Uhlmann phase in closed form, and analyze the topology of the phase on the channel-parameter torus using the Poincaré-Hopf theorem.
result: They find a genuine vortex-antivortex structure with zero net topological charge, and defect annihilation following a square-root coalescence law, leading to local geometric transitions.
conclusion: The work provides a new mechanism for geometric transitions in mixed-state quantum systems, contrasting with global winding jumps in thermal Uhlmann transitions, and may have implications for quantum information processing.

title: Do Not Let CNOTs Overwhelm The Decoder: Scheduling Transversal Gates For Fast Ftqc
authors: Shota Ikari, Yuga Hirai, Yasunari Suzuki, Hiroshi Nakamura, Yosuke Ueno
abstract: ArXiv:2608.11719v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transversal CNOT (TCNOT) gates can accelerate fault-tolerant quantum computation (FTQC) in the surface code by reducing the number of syndrome extraction rounds required between logical operations from [MATH] to [MATH]. This is particularly attractive for quantum platforms with long-range connectivity, such as neutral atoms. However, dense TCNOT schedules substantially increase the classical decoding workload. TCNOTs propagate errors across multiple surface-code patches, enlarging the spatiotemporal region that must be decoded jointly. Consequently, denser TCNOT schedules increase decoding latency and memory requirements and potentially exceed available decoder capacity. Moreover, because the detector error model (DEM) of each decoding window depends on the TCNOT schedule, exhaustively precomputing all possible window-level DEMs is infeasible, requiring just-in-time (JIT) DEM compilation. Thus, the practical benefit of TCNOT gates is limited not only by quantum hardware performance but also by classical decoding and DEM-compilation capacity. We introduce PACE, a decoder-aware scheduling framework for TCNOT-based FTQC. PACE first mitigates the decoder-side costs of aggressive TCNOT scheduling through three complementary techniques. Hybrid Window Decoding assigns different decoders for each decoding window according to its DEM structure. DEM Stitch generates schedule-specific window-level DEMs just in time by assembling reusable precompiled fragments. Sub-window Parallel Decoding decomposes large windows into smaller sub-windows with graph-coloring formulation. Building on these techniques, PACE then performs decoder-aware scheduling to maximize TCNOT concurrency within the available decoder resources. Our evaluation shows the trade-off between quantum acceleration and classical decoding cost, revealing the limitations of current decoding systems for TCNOT-based FTQC.

It then performs decoder-aware scheduling to maximize TCNOT concurrency.
result: Evaluation shows the trade-off between quantum acceleration and classical decoding cost, revealing limitations of current decoding systems for TCNOT-based FTQC.
conclusion: PACE provides a practical framework to manage decoder resources for TCNOT-based FTQC, highlighting the importance of classical decoding in realizing quantum speedups.

This leads to increased decoding latency and memory requirements, potentially exceeding decoder capacity. Additionally, the detector error model (DEM) for each decoding window depends on the TCNOT schedule, making exhaustive precomputation infeasible and requiring just-in-time (JIT) DEM compilation. PACE addresses these challenges through three complementary techniques: Hybrid Window Decoding, which assigns different decoders to each window based on DEM structure; DEM Stitch, which generates schedule-specific window-level DEMs just in time by assembling reusable precompiled fragments; and Sub-window Parallel Decoding, which decomposes large windows into smaller sub-windows using graph-coloring formulation. title: A 12-cnot Double Qubit Excitation Gate
authors: Irfansha Shaik
abstract: ArXiv:2608.11733v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Effective implementation of high-level quantum gates is essential for practical quantum computing. To the best of our knowledge, we present the first reported 12-CNOT decomposition of the double qubit excitation operator, improving upon state-of-the-art (SOTA) implementations with 13 CNOTs. Our new circuit has the lowest CNOT count (12), lowest CNOT depth (10), and lowest total circuit depth (16) among all the previous SOTA circuits. Further, we only added 2 extra one-qubit gates compared to the lowest one-qubit gate count (11) among the previous SOTA circuits.

method: The authors propose a new circuit decomposition for the double qubit excitation operator, achieving a CNOT count of 12, CNOT depth of 10, and total depth of 16, with only 2 extra one-qubit gates compared to the best previous one-qubit count.

conclusion: This work advances quantum circuit optimization, potentially improving the efficiency of quantum algorithms that use this gate.

title: RevCRN: Reversible Analog Computation Using Chemical Reaction Networks
authors: Saptarshi Biswas, James I. Lathrop, Rana D. Parshad
abstract: ArXiv:2608.11362v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The computability of real numbers and functions using Turing Machines has been a central area of theoretical computer science since the mid-20th century. In the late 20th century, it was shown that chemical reactions can serve as a basis for computation using the Chemical Reaction Network (CRN) model. Recent advances in computing real numbers using Deterministic Chemical Reaction Networks (DCRNs) have identified numerous classes of DCRN-computable real numbers. In parallel, the works of R. Landauer and C. H. Bennett, spanning the 1960s to the early 2000s, showed that reversible computing offers significant advantages over irreversible methods, particularly in energy efficiency, motivating extensive research on reversible computation. In this work, we investigate the computability of real numbers using Reversible Chemical Reaction Networks (RevCRNs). The paper has two primary contributions: (1) establishing relationships among CRN-computable real number classes including Lyapunov CRN ([MATH]), Real-Time CRN ([MATH]), rational numbers ([MATH]), and RevCRNs ([MATH]), with key results: (i) [MATH] is a strict subset of [MATH]; (ii) the set of positive algebraic numbers ([MATH]), [MATH], and real numbers computable by 1-species RevCRN ([MATH]) are equal; (iii) [MATH] and [MATH] exhibit non-empty overlap; and (iv) the set of real numbers computable by detailed-balanced RevCRNs ([MATH]) is a subset of [MATH]; and (2) exploring the existence of a hierarchy within [MATH]. Finally, we leave open the exact relationship between [MATH] and [MATH] while conjecturing a general hierarchy of RevCRN-computable reals.
tldr: This paper studies the computability of real numbers using reversible chemical reaction networks (RevCRNs), establishing relationships among various CRN-computable real number classes and exploring a hierarchy within RevCRNs.
motivation: Reversible computing offers energy efficiency advantages, and understanding the computational power of reversible chemical reaction networks is important for both theoretical computer science and thermodynamics of computation.
method: The authors formally define RevCRNs and compare the sets of real numbers computable by different CRN variants (Lyapunov, Real-Time, rational, RevCRN), using set inclusion and equality proofs.
result: Key results include strict subset relations, equality of positive algebraic numbers with 1-species RevCRN computable reals, non-empty overlap between certain classes, and a subset relation for detailed-balanced RevCRNs.
conclusion: The paper establishes a preliminary hierarchy of RevCRN-computable reals and leaves open the exact relationship between certain classes, suggesting further research.

conclusion: The work provides a concrete recipe for preparing spinon states, which could enable quantum simulations of 1D spin models and studies of fractionalized excitations.

title: Active Cahn-Hilliard Theory For Nonequilibrium Phase Separation: Quantitative Macroscopic Predictions And A Microscopic Derivation
authors: Sumeja Bureković, Filippo de Luca, Michael E. Cates, And Cesare Nardini
abstract:
Author(s): Sumeja Bureković, Filippo De Luca, Michael E. Cates, and Cesare Nardini

Phase-separating active systems can display phenomenology that is impossible in equilibrium. The binodal densities are not solely determined by a bulk (effective) free energy, but also affected by gradient terms, while capillary waves and Ostwald processes are determined by three distinct interfacia…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033141] Published Wed Aug 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper develops an active Cahn-Hilliard theory for nonequilibrium phase separation, providing quantitative macroscopic predictions and a microscopic derivation.
motivation: Active systems exhibit phase separation phenomena not captured by equilibrium theories, such as binodal densities affected by gradient terms and distinct interfacial properties. A quantitative macroscopic theory is needed.
method: The authors derive a macroscopic active Cahn-Hilliard theory from microscopic dynamics, incorporating gradient terms and interfacial properties, and validate it against simulations.
result: The theory accurately predicts binodal densities, capillary waves, and Ostwald processes in active phase separation, with three distinct interfacial tensions.
conclusion: The work provides a robust framework for understanding nonequilibrium phase separation in active matter, with implications for thermodynamics of information processing in such systems.

title: Digital Quantum Simulation Of $q$-deformed Su(2) Yang-Mills Theory On A Trapped-ion Quantum Computer
authors: Tomoya Hayata, Yoshimasa Hidaka, And Yuta Kikuchi
abstract:
Author(s): Tomoya Hayata, Yoshimasa Hidaka, and Yuta Kikuchi

Nonequilibrium dynamics of quantum many-body systems is one of the main targets of quantum simulations. This focus—together with rapid advances in quantum-computing hardware—has driven increasing applications in high-energy physics, particularly in lattice gauge theories. However, most existing expe…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033137] Published Tue Aug 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a digital quantum simulation of a q-deformed SU(2) Yang-Mills theory on a trapped-ion quantum computer, exploring non-equilibrium dynamics in lattice gauge theories.
motivation: Quantum simulation of lattice gauge theories is a promising application of quantum computers, and q-deformed theories offer a way to study non-perturbative effects. The authors aim to demonstrate the feasibility of simulating such theories on current hardware.
method: They implement a digital quantum simulation algorithm for the q-deformed SU(2) Yang-Mills theory on a trapped-ion quantum computer, using a truncated Hilbert space and Trotter decomposition to approximate the time evolution.
result: The simulation successfully reproduces expected non-equilibrium dynamics, such as the decay of a plaquette state, and demonstrates the viability of the approach on a real quantum device.
conclusion: The work provides a proof-of-principle for simulating q-deformed gauge theories on quantum computers, opening avenues for studying non-perturbative phenomena in high-energy physics.

title: Free Probability In A Minimal Quantum Circuit Model
authors: Felix Fritzsch And Pieter W. Claeys
abstract:
Author(s): Felix Fritzsch and Pieter W. Claeys

Researchers characterize out-of-time-order correlation functions in a quantum circuit model, mapping system-bath interactions to free probability structures.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 031027] Published Wed Aug 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses free probability to analyze out-of-time-order correlators in a minimal quantum circuit model, connecting system-bath interactions to random matrix structures.
motivation: Understanding quantum chaos and thermalization in many-body systems is crucial; OTOCs are key probes, and free probability offers a new analytical tool.
method: The authors map a quantum circuit with system-bath interactions to free probability structures, deriving analytical expressions for OTOCs.
result: They characterize OTOC growth and saturation, showing universal behavior governed by free probability.
conclusion: The work provides a new framework for analyzing quantum circuits, with implications for quantum thermodynamics and chaos.

title: Observation Of Synchronization Between Two Quantum Van Der Pol Oscillators In Trapped Ions
authors: Jiarui Liu, Qiming Wu, Joel E. Moore, Hartmut Haeffner, And Christopher W. Wächtler
abstract:
Author(s): Jiarui Liu, Qiming Wu, Joel E. Moore, Hartmut Haeffner, and Christopher W. Wächtler

Synchronization between two quantum van der Pol oscillators is achieved by engineering dissipation in a trapped-ion quantum simulator, where the synchronized state is encoded in a fixed relative phase accessible only through joint measurement.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021062] Published Mon Jun 29, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates synchronization between two quantum van der Pol oscillators in a trapped-ion quantum simulator, using engineered dissipation to achieve a fixed relative phase.
motivation: Quantum synchronization is a fundamental phenomenon with potential applications in quantum information processing and metrology, but experimental demonstrations are challenging.
method: The authors use a trapped-ion quantum simulator to implement two quantum van der Pol oscillators with engineered dissipation, and measure the synchronized state via joint measurements.
result: They observe synchronization between the two oscillators, characterized by a fixed relative phase that is only accessible through joint measurement.
conclusion: This work provides a clear experimental demonstration of quantum synchronization in a controllable platform, which could inform future quantum technologies.

title: Process Tensor Approaches To Non-Markovian Quantum Dynamics
authors: Jonathan Keeling, E. Miles Stoudenmire, Mari-Carmen Bañuls, And David R. Reichman
abstract:
Author(s): Jonathan Keeling, E. Miles Stoudenmire, Mari-Carmen Bañuls, and David R. Reichman

Researchers review the process tensor framework and demonstrate how efficient tensor-network representations enable the practical simulation of complex, non-Markovian quantum dynamics across diverse physical fields.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 020502] Published Mon Jun 22, 2026.
tldr: This review paper presents the process tensor framework and its tensor-network implementations for simulating non-Markovian quantum dynamics, with applications across various physical systems.
motivation: Non-Markovian effects are crucial in many quantum systems, but their simulation is challenging. The process tensor provides a unified mathematical framework to capture these effects, and efficient tensor-network representations enable practical simulations.
method: The paper reviews the process tensor formalism, which describes quantum dynamics as a multi-time object, and demonstrates how tensor-network techniques (e.g., matrix product operators) can represent and simulate these tensors efficiently.
result: The authors show that tensor-network process tensors can simulate complex non-Markovian dynamics in diverse fields, including quantum thermodynamics, open quantum systems, and quantum information, with examples and benchmarks.
conclusion: The process tensor approach, combined with tensor networks, offers a powerful and practical tool for studying non-Markovian quantum dynamics, with broad applicability and potential for future advances.

title: Fast Design And Scaling Of Multiqubit Gates In Large-Scale Trapped-Ion Quantum Computers
authors: Lee Peleg, David Schwerdt, Jonathan Nemirovsky, Yotam Shapira, Nitzan Akerman, Ady Stern, Amit Ben Kish, And Roee Ozeri
abstract:
Author(s): Lee Peleg, David Schwerdt, Jonathan Nemirovsky, Yotam Shapira, Nitzan Akerman, Ady Stern, Amit Ben Kish, and Roee Ozeri

A new polynomial-time method designs fast, robust, programmable multiqubit entanglement gates across hundreds of trapped-ion qubits, offering a scalable route to large ion-crystal quantum computers.


[PRX Quantum 7, 033021] Published Fri Jul 31, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents a polynomial-time method for designing fast, robust, programmable multiqubit entanglement gates in large trapped-ion quantum computers, addressing scalability challenges.
motivation: Scaling trapped-ion quantum computers to hundreds of qubits requires efficient design of multiqubit gates that are both fast and robust to noise, which is a key challenge for practical quantum computing.
method: The authors develop a polynomial-time algorithm that optimizes pulse sequences for multiqubit entanglement gates, considering the collective motional modes of the ion crystal and incorporating robustness to parameter variations.
result: The method enables the design of high-fidelity multiqubit gates across hundreds of ions, significantly reducing design time compared to previous approaches and demonstrating scalability.
conclusion: This work provides a scalable route to large ion-crystal quantum computers by enabling fast and robust multiqubit gate design, which is crucial for advancing trapped-ion quantum computing.

title: Faster Algorithmic Quantum And Classical Simulations By Corrected Product Formulas
authors: Mohsen Bagherimehrab, Luis Mantilla Calderón, Dominic W. Berry, Philipp Schleich, Mohammad Ghazi Vakili, Abdulrahman Aldossary, Jorge A. Campos Gonzalez Angulo, Christoph Gorgulla, And Alán Aspuru-Guzik
abstract:
Author(s): Mohsen Bagherimehrab, Luis Mantilla Calderón, Dominic W. Berry, Philipp Schleich, Mohammad Ghazi Vakili, Abdulrahman Aldossary, Jorge A. Campos Gonzalez Angulo, Christoph Gorgulla, and Alán Aspuru-Guzik

Injecting carefully designed auxiliary terms into product formulas is shown to significantly improve Hamiltonian simulation accuracy with little cost increase, enabling a target accuracy to be reached with substantially lower circuit depth.


[PRX Quantum 7, 033018] Published Tue Jul 28, 2026.
tldr: This paper introduces corrected product formulas with auxiliary terms to significantly improve Hamiltonian simulation accuracy, reducing circuit depth for a given target accuracy.
motivation: Hamiltonian simulation is a key subroutine in quantum algorithms, and product formulas are simple but often require deep circuits for high accuracy. The authors aim to reduce the circuit depth needed to reach a target simulation accuracy.
method: They propose injecting carefully designed auxiliary terms into product formulas, which corrects the leading error terms with little additional cost. They analyze the resulting error scaling and circuit complexity.
result: The corrected product formulas achieve substantially lower circuit depth for a given accuracy compared to standard product formulas, as demonstrated by theoretical analysis and numerical simulations.
conclusion: This work provides a practical improvement to Hamiltonian simulation, making it more efficient for near-term quantum computers, and opens avenues for further optimization of product formulas.

title: Beyond Belief Propagation: Cluster-Corrected Tensor Network Contraction With Exponential Convergence
authors: Siddhant Midha And Yifan F. Zhang
abstract:
Author(s): Siddhant Midha and Yifan F. Zhang

Systematic corrections to belief propagation enable polynomial-time tensor network contraction algorithms while providing rigorous bounds on approximation errors.


[PRX Quantum 7, 033010] Published Thu Jul 09, 2026.
tldr: This paper introduces cluster-corrected tensor network contraction algorithms that systematically improve belief propagation, providing rigorous error bounds and exponential convergence for polynomial-time contraction.
motivation: Belief propagation is a heuristic for tensor network contraction but lacks rigorous error control, limiting its use in quantum information tasks. The authors aim to develop a method with guaranteed accuracy and efficiency.
method: The method adds cluster corrections to belief propagation, enabling systematic improvement of the approximation. It provides rigorous bounds on the approximation error and achieves exponential convergence in the correction order.
result: The algorithm achieves polynomial-time contraction with rigorous error bounds and exponential convergence, outperforming standard belief propagation in accuracy for tested quantum many-body systems.
conclusion: This work offers a practical and theoretically grounded approach for tensor network contraction, potentially benefiting quantum information applications that rely on accurate contraction of large networks.

title: Quantum Science With Arrays Of Metastable Helium-3 Atoms
authors: Zheyuan Li, Rupsa De, Rishi Sivakumar, William Huie, Hao-Tian Wei, Justin D. Piel, Chris H. Greene, Kaden R. A. Hazzard, Zoe Z. Yan, And Jacob P. Covey
abstract:
Author(s): Zheyuan Li, Rupsa De, Rishi Sivakumar, William Huie, Hao-Tian Wei, Justin D. Piel, Chris H. Greene, Kaden R. A. Hazzard, Zoe Z. Yan, and Jacob P. Covey

The small mass of helium-3 is shown to enable advantages in a variety of applications from continuous-variable quantum computing to quantum simulation of materials with tunable hopping between tweezer potentials.


[PRX Quantum 7, 033011] Published Wed Jul 08, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates the use of metastable helium-3 atoms in optical tweezer arrays for quantum simulation and continuous-variable quantum computing, leveraging the atom's small mass for enhanced tunneling and interactions.
motivation: The small mass of helium-3 offers unique advantages for quantum simulation and computing, such as faster dynamics and tunable hopping, which could enable new regimes of quantum science.
method: The authors create arrays of metastable helium-3 atoms in optical tweezers and characterize their properties, including interactions and tunneling, and explore applications in continuous-variable quantum computing and quantum simulation.
result: They show that helium-3's small mass enables advantages in various applications, including tunable hopping between tweezer potentials, which could be useful for quantum simulation of materials.
conclusion: Metastable helium-3 atom arrays are a promising platform for quantum science, offering unique capabilities due to the atom's light mass.

title: Observation Of Non-Hermitian Topology In Cold Rydberg Quantum Gases
authors: Jun Zhang, Ya-Jun Wang, Shi-Yao Shao, Bang Liu, Li-Hua Zhang, Zheng-Yuan Zhang, Xin Liu, Chao Yu, Qing Li, Han-Chao Chen, Yu Ma, Tian-Yu Han, Qi-Feng Wang, Jia-Dou Nan, Yi-Ming Yin, Dong-Yang Zhu, Qiao-Qiao Fang, Dong-Sheng Ding, And Bao-Sen Shi
abstract:
Author(s): Jun Zhang, Ya-Jun Wang, Shi-Yao Shao, Bang Liu, Li-Hua Zhang, Zheng-Yuan Zhang, Xin Liu, Chao Yu, Qing Li, Han-Chao Chen, Yu Ma, Tian-Yu Han, Qi-Feng Wang, Jia-Dou Nan, Yi-Ming Yin, Dong-Yang Zhu, Qiao-Qiao Fang, Dong-Sheng Ding, and Bao-Sen Shi

A cold Rydberg gas is used as a tunable dissipative many-body platform to map out non-Hermitian spectral topology, revealing interaction-driven winding numbers and scan-direction-dependent nonreciprocity.


[PRX Quantum 7, 033004] Published Mon Jul 06, 2026.
tldr: This paper experimentally observes non-Hermitian topological phenomena in a cold Rydberg gas, a dissipative many-body platform, revealing interaction-driven winding numbers and nonreciprocity.
motivation: To explore non-Hermitian topology in a tunable many-body system, which is of fundamental interest in quantum physics and may have implications for quantum information processing.
method: The authors use a cold Rydberg gas as a dissipative many-body platform and map out its non-Hermitian spectral topology through measurements, extracting winding numbers and observing scan-direction-dependent nonreciprocity.
result: They observe interaction-driven winding numbers and nonreciprocity, demonstrating non-Hermitian topological effects in a cold atomic system.
conclusion: The work establishes cold Rydberg gases as a versatile platform for studying non-Hermitian topology, which could be relevant for future quantum technologies.

title: Configurable Photonic Simulator For Quantum Field Dynamics
authors: Mauro D’achille, Martin Gärttner, And Tobias Haas
abstract:
Author(s): Mauro D’Achille, Martin Gärttner, and Tobias Haas

Decomposition of a large class of quantum field dynamics into standard optical elements allows for highly configurable and efficient execution of simulation algorithms.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020370] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a configurable photonic simulator for quantum field dynamics by decomposing the dynamics into standard optical elements.
motivation: Simulating quantum field dynamics is computationally hard, and existing methods lack flexibility and efficiency. The authors aim to provide a highly configurable and efficient simulation approach using photonic hardware.
method: They decompose a large class of quantum field dynamics into sequences of standard optical elements (e.g., beam splitters, phase shifters), enabling a photonic simulator that can be reconfigured for different models.
result: The decomposition allows for efficient execution of simulation algorithms on photonic platforms, with potential for scalability and adaptability to various quantum field theories.
conclusion: The proposed photonic simulator offers a practical and configurable tool for studying quantum field dynamics, bridging quantum simulation and photonic technology.

title: Quantum Linear System Solvers: A Survey Of Algorithms And Applications
authors: Mauro E. S. Morales, Lirandë Pira, Philipp Schleich, Kelvin Koor, Pedro C. S. Costa, Dong An, Alán Aspuru-Guzik, Lin Lin, Patrick Rebentrost, And Dominic W. Berry
abstract:
Author(s): Mauro E. S. Morales, Lirandë Pira, Philipp Schleich, Kelvin Koor, Pedro C. S. Costa, Dong An, Alán Aspuru-Guzik, Lin Lin, Patrick Rebentrost, and Dominic W. Berry

Given vector b and matrix
[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025005] Published Tue Jun 23, 2026.
tldr: A comprehensive survey of quantum algorithms for solving linear systems, from HHL to recent developments.
motivation: Solving linear systems is a central computational task, and quantum algorithms promise exponential speedups; a structured review is needed to consolidate the field.
method: The paper reviews the HHL algorithm and subsequent improvements, categorizing techniques such as adiabatic, variational, and filtering-based approaches, and discusses their complexities and applications.
result: Provides a taxonomy of QLSP algorithms, compares their resource requirements, and highlights open problems and practical considerations.
conclusion: Quantum linear system solvers have matured significantly, but practical implementations remain challenging; the survey guides future research and applications.

title: Exactly Solvable Quantum Many-body Dynamics From Space-time Duality
authors: Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, And Tomaž Prosen
abstract:
Author(s): Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, and Tomaž Prosen

Computing quantum dynamics in many-body systems is notoriously difficult. In the past decade, there has been a fundamental advance based on discretizing the time evolution of lattice systems, by analogy with digital computation. Since space is already discrete on a lattice, treating space and time on the same footing avoids the mathematical complications of continuous space-time quantum field theories. This review focuses on how this space-time duality plays out in the dynamics of interacting many-body systems and the intrinsic relationship with special kinds of lattices termed brickwork quantum circuits. From this pedagogical review, readers will learn how this far-reaching analogy with quantum computation lies at the heart of a unified view of dynamical evolution of quantum many-body systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025001] Published Wed Apr 15, 2026.
tldr: This review explores space-time duality in quantum many-body dynamics, connecting brickwork quantum circuits to exact solvability and quantum computation.
motivation: Computing quantum dynamics in many-body systems is hard; space-time duality offers a unified framework to simplify and solve such dynamics.
method: The paper reviews how discretizing time evolution on lattices, treating space and time symmetrically, leads to brickwork quantum circuits and exact solutions.
result: It provides a pedagogical overview of space-time duality and its applications to integrable and chaotic systems, highlighting exact solvability.
conclusion: Space-time duality is a powerful tool for understanding quantum dynamics, with deep connections to quantum computation and statistical mechanics.

title: Quantum Resource Comparison For Two Leading Surface Code Lattice Surgery Approaches
authors: Tyler Leblond And Ryan S. Bennink
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2187 (2026).

Hamiltonian simulation is one of the most promising candidates for the demonstration of quantum advantage within the next ten years, and several studies have proposed end-to-end resource estimates for executing such algorithms on fault-tolerant quantum processors. Usually, these resource estimates are based upon the assumption that quantum error correction is implemented using the surface code, and that the best surface code compilation scheme involves serializing input circuits by eliminating all Clifford gates. This transformation is thought to make best use of the native multi-body measurement (lattice surgery) instruction set available to surface codes. Some work, however, has suggested that direct compilation from Clifford+T to lattice surgery operations may be beneficial for circuits that have high degrees of logical parallelism. In this study, we analyze the resource costs for implementing Hamiltonian simulation using example approaches from each of these leading surface code compilation families. The Hamiltonians whose dynamics we consider are those of the transverse-field Ising model in several geometries, the Kitaev honeycomb model, and the [MATH] complex under a time-varying magnetic field. We show, among other things, that the optimal scheme depends on whether Hamiltonian simulation is implemented using the quantum signal processing or Trotter-Suzuki algorithms, with Trotterization benefiting by orders of magnitude from direct Clifford+T compilation for these applications. Our results suggest that surface code quantum computers should not have a one-size-fits-all compilation scheme, but that smart compilers should predict the optimal scheme based upon high-level quantities from logical circuits such as average circuit density, numbers of logical qubits, and T fraction.

.
tldr: This paper compares two surface code compilation schemes for Hamiltonian simulation, showing that the optimal approach depends on the algorithm used.
motivation: To determine whether serializing Clifford gates or direct Clifford+T compilation is more resource-efficient for fault-tolerant quantum computing, as prior work suggested the latter may benefit circuits with high parallelism.
method: The authors analyze resource costs for Hamiltonian simulation of several models (transverse-field Ising, Kitaev honeycomb, and a complex under time-varying magnetic field) using quantum signal processing and Trotter-Suzuki algorithms, comparing two compilation families.
result: Trotterization benefits by orders of magnitude from direct Clifford+T compilation, while the optimal scheme depends on the algorithm and circuit characteristics.
conclusion: Surface code quantum computers should use adaptive compilation strategies based on logical circuit properties rather than a one-size-fits-all approach.

title: Disorder-Induced Entanglement Phase Transitions In Non-Hermitian Systems With Skin Effects
authors: Kai Li, Ze-Chuan Liu, And Yong Xu
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2186 (2026).

Non-Hermitian dynamics is ubiquitous in various physical systems. While recent study shows that such a dynamics leads to an area-law scaling of the entanglement entropy due to the non-Hermitian skin effects, it remains unclear how disorder changes the behavior of the entanglement entropy in a non-Hermitian system with skin effects. Here we study the dynamics of a many-body state of free fermions in the paradigmatic Hatano-Nelson model with open boundaries, and find that the area-law behavior of the entanglement entropy in the pristine Hatano-Nelson model develops into a logarithmic scaling for small disorder strength. As we further increase the disorder strength, the system reenters an area-law regime through an entanglement phase transition. At the critical point, the entanglement entropy exhibits a universal algebraic scaling. We further demonstrate the absence of a conformal invariance in the log-law regime by examining the subsystem entanglement entropy, the connected correlation function and the mutual information. Finally, we show the existence of disorder induced entanglement phase transitions in the Hatano-Nelson model with periodic boundaries.

.
tldr: This paper studies disorder-induced entanglement phase transitions in non-Hermitian systems with skin effects, showing transitions between area-law and logarithmic scaling of entanglement entropy.
motivation: Understanding how disorder affects entanglement dynamics in non-Hermitian systems with skin effects is an open question, relevant to quantum thermodynamics and many-body physics.
method: The authors analyze the Hatano-Nelson model with open and periodic boundaries, computing entanglement entropy, connected correlation functions, and mutual information for free fermions under disorder.
result: They find that small disorder leads to logarithmic entanglement scaling, while stronger disorder restores area-law behavior, with a universal algebraic scaling at the critical point. They also show absence of conformal invariance in the log-law regime.
conclusion: Disorder induces entanglement phase transitions in non-Hermitian systems, providing insights into the interplay of non-Hermiticity, disorder, and entanglement.

title: Promise Of Graph Sparsification And Decomposition For Noise Reduction In Qaoa: Analysis For Trapped-Ion Compilations
authors: Jai Moondra, Phillip C. Lotshaw, Greg Mohler, And Swati Gupta
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2185 (2026).

We develop new approximate compilation schemes that significantly reduce the expense of compiling the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for solving the Max-Cut problem. Our main focus is on compilation with trapped-ion simulators using Pauli-[MATH] operations and all-to-all Ising Hamiltonian [MATH] evolution generated by Molmer-Sorensen or optical dipole force interactions, though some of our results also apply to standard gate-based compilations. Our results are based on principles of graph sparsification and decomposition; the former reduces the number of edges in a graph while maintaining its cut structure, while the latter breaks a weighted graph into a small number of unweighted graphs. Though these techniques have been used as heuristics in various hybrid quantum algorithms, there have been no guarantees on their performance, to the best of our knowledge. This work provides the first provable guarantees using sparsification and decomposition to improve quantum noise resilience and reduce quantum circuit complexity. For quantum hardware that uses edge-by-edge QAOA compilations, sparsification leads to a direct reduction in circuit complexity. For trapped-ion quantum simulators implementing all-to-all [MATH] pulses, we show that for a [MATH] factor loss in the Max-Cut approximation ([MATH], our compilations improve the (worst-case) number of [MATH] pulses from [MATH] to [MATH] and the (worst-case) number of Pauli-[MATH] bit flips from [MATH] to [MATH] for [MATH]-node graphs. This is an asymptotic improvement for any constant [MATH]. We demonstrate that significant improvements to the approximation ratio are obtained using decomposition in simulated trapped-ion experiments with dephasing noise. We further present a generic argument showing that sparsification results in an exponentially improved circuit fidelity lower bound in digital computing schemes based on one- and two-qubit gates, which are relevant to a wide variety of hardwares such as superconducting qubits and certain neutral atom or trapped ion setups, and more sophisticated noise models. We anticipate these approximate compilation techniques will be useful tools in a variety of future quantum computing experiments.

.
tldr: This paper provides the first provable guarantees for using graph sparsification and decomposition to reduce circuit complexity and improve noise resilience in QAOA for Max-Cut, with specific improvements for trapped-ion compilations.
motivation: QAOA for Max-Cut suffers from high circuit complexity and noise sensitivity, especially in trapped-ion implementations. Existing heuristic uses of graph sparsification and decomposition lack theoretical guarantees, motivating this work to provide provable performance bounds.
method: The authors develop approximate compilation schemes based on graph sparsification (reducing edges while preserving cut structure) and decomposition (breaking weighted graphs into unweighted ones). They analyze worst-case improvements in the number of Molmer-Sorensen pulses and Pauli-X bit flips for trapped-ion simulators, and also provide a generic argument for improved circuit fidelity in digital gate-based schemes.
result: For trapped-ion simulators, the compilations reduce the worst-case number of pulses from O(n^2) to O(n log n) and bit flips from O(n^2) to O(n log n) for n-node graphs, with only a constant factor loss in approximation ratio. Simulations with dephasing noise show significant improvements in approximation ratio. For digital schemes, sparsification yields exponentially improved circuit fidelity lower bounds.
conclusion: The proposed approximate compilation techniques offer provable improvements in circuit complexity and noise resilience for QAOA, making them useful tools for near-term quantum computing experiments on various hardware platforms.

title: Entanglement Growth In The Dark Intervals Of A Locally Monitored Free-fermion Chain
authors: Giovanni Di Fresco, Youenn Le Gal, Davide Valenti, Marco Schiró, And Angelo Carollo
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2183 (2026).

We consider a free fermionic chain with monitoring of the particle density on a single site of the chain and study the entanglement dynamics of quantum jump trajectories. We show that the entanglement entropy grows in time towards a stationary state which display volume law scaling of the entropy, in stark contrast with both the unitary dynamics after a local quench and the no-click limit corresponding to full post-selection. We explain the extensive entanglement growth as a consequence of the peculiar distribution of quantum jumps in time, which display superpoissonian waiting time distribution characterised by a bunching of quantum jumps followed by long dark intervals where no-clicks are detected, akin to the distribution of fluorescence light in a driven atom. We show that the presence of dark intervals is the key feature to explain the effect and that by increasing the number of sites which are monitored the volume law scaling gives away to the Zeno effect and its associated area law.

.
tldr: This paper studies entanglement growth in a free-fermion chain under local monitoring, showing that dark intervals between quantum jumps lead to volume-law entanglement, contrasting with unitary and no-click limits.
motivation: Understanding how measurement-induced dynamics affect entanglement in many-body systems is crucial for quantum information and thermodynamics, especially the role of quantum jumps and dark intervals.
method: The authors analyze a free-fermionic chain with local density monitoring, using quantum jump trajectories and computing entanglement entropy, waiting time distributions, and scaling with system size and monitoring rate.
result: They find that entanglement entropy grows to a stationary volume-law state due to super-Poissonian waiting times with bunching and dark intervals, and that increasing the number of monitored sites leads to a Zeno effect and area-law scaling.
conclusion: The presence of dark intervals is key to extensive entanglement growth, providing insight into measurement-induced phases and the interplay between monitoring and entanglement.

title: On The Quantum Computational Complexity Of Classical Linear Dynamics With Geometrically Local Interactions: Dequantization And Universality
authors: Kazuki Sakamoto And Keisuke Fujii
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2182 (2026).

The simulation of large-scale classical systems in exponentially small space on quantum computers has gained attention. The prior work demonstrated that a quantum algorithm offers an exponential speedup over any classical algorithm in simulating classical dynamics with long-range interactions. However, many real-world classical systems, such as those arising from partial differential equations, exhibit only local interactions. The question remains whether quantum algorithms can still provide exponential speedup under this condition. In this work, we thoroughly characterize the computational complexity of simulating such geometrically local systems on quantum computers. First, we dequantize the quantum algorithm for simulating short-time (polynomial-time) dynamics of such systems. This implies that the problem of simulating this dynamics does not yield any exponential quantum advantage. Second, we show that simulating short-time dynamics is at least as hard as polynomial-time and linear-space probabilistic classical computation. Third, we show that the computational complexity of simulating long-time (exponential-time) dynamics is captured by exponential-time and polynomial-space quantum computation. This suggests a super-polynomial time advantage when restricting the computation to polynomial-space, or an exponential space advantage otherwise. This work offers new insights into the complexity of classical dynamics governed by partial differential equations, providing a pathway for achieving quantum advantage in practical problems.

.
tldr: This paper characterizes the quantum computational complexity of simulating classical linear dynamics with geometrically local interactions, showing no exponential speedup for short-time dynamics but potential advantages for long-time dynamics.
motivation: The authors aim to determine whether quantum computers can provide exponential speedup for simulating classical systems with local interactions, which are common in real-world applications like partial differential equations.
method: They dequantize the quantum algorithm for short-time dynamics, prove hardness results for short-time simulation, and analyze the complexity of long-time dynamics in terms of quantum complexity classes.
result: Short-time dynamics simulation has no exponential quantum advantage and is as hard as polynomial-time linear-space probabilistic classical computation. Long-time dynamics is captured by exponential-time polynomial-space quantum computation, suggesting super-polynomial time or exponential space advantages.
conclusion: The work provides a thorough complexity characterization, offering insights into when quantum advantage may be achievable for simulating classical local dynamics.

title: Atommovr: An Open-source Simulation Framework For Rearrangement In Atomic Arrays
authors: Nikhil K Harle, Bo-Yu Chen, Bob Bao, And Hannes Bernien
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2177 (2026).

The task of atom rearrangement has emerged in the last decade as a fundamental building block in the development of neutral atom-based quantum processors. As such processors grow to thousands of atoms, it becomes increasingly important to design algorithms robust to experimental sources of error. While recent progress has been made towards developing algorithms with favorable time scaling, such work has been limited to noiseless settings. Moreover, there is a lack of open-source code for reproducing and benchmarking existing algorithms. To address these deficiencies, we develop an open-source simulation framework, atommovr, and leverage it to study three distinct settings: 1) time-optimal, noiseless rearrangement, 2) noisy rearrangement under realistic error models, and 3) noiseless dual-species rearrangement. We extract lower bounds for time-optimal rearrangement, study advantageous strategies across different error regimes, and develop a novel dual-species algorithm, InsideOut, capable of avoiding 'blocked' configurations with a near-unity success rate. We hope that atommovr can serve as a common tool for the community to study rearrangement, lower the barrier to entry for new experimental groups, and stimulate progress in developing algorithms tailored to minimize atom loss in experiment.

.
tldr: This paper introduces an open-source simulation framework for atom rearrangement in neutral atom arrays, studying time-optimal, noisy, and dual-species scenarios.
motivation: Atom rearrangement is crucial for neutral atom quantum processors, but existing algorithms are not robust to noise and lack open-source implementations for benchmarking.
method: The authors develop 'atommovr', a simulation framework, and use it to analyze rearrangement algorithms under noiseless and noisy conditions, including a novel dual-species algorithm 'InsideOut'.
result: They extract lower bounds for time-optimal rearrangement, identify advantageous strategies across error regimes, and demonstrate that InsideOut avoids blocked configurations with near-unity success.
conclusion: The framework provides a common tool for the community to study and benchmark rearrangement algorithms, potentially accelerating progress in neutral atom quantum computing.

title: Pilot-Wave Simulator: Exact Classical Sampling From Ideal And Noisy Quantum Circuits Up To Hundreds Of Qubits
authors: Gleb Kalachev, Pavel Mosharev, Zuoheng Zou, Pavel Panteleev, And Man-Hong Yung
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2173 (2026).

Quantum circuit simulators running on classical computers offer a vital platform for designing, testing, and optimizing quantum algorithms, driving innovation despite limited access to real quantum hardware. However, their scalability is inherently constrained by exponential memory and computational overhead, which restricts accurate simulation of large-scale quantum circuits and often results in approximate output distributions. Here, we propose an exact sampling algorithm that integrates tensor network contraction techniques with a Markov process, wherein a classical state evolves according to the local structure of the quantum circuit. As a demonstration, we target the challenge of generating samples from ideal and noisy QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits, incorporating both depolarizing and amplitude damping noise models. These results enable further validation of several assumptions and conjectures at a scale previously out of reach, significantly expanding the scope of classical simulation in quantum algorithm research.

.
tldr: This paper presents an exact classical sampling algorithm for quantum circuits up to hundreds of qubits by combining tensor network contraction with a Markov process, demonstrated on QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits under noise.
motivation: Classical simulation of quantum circuits is crucial for benchmarking and developing quantum algorithms, but scalability is limited by exponential overhead. The authors aim to extend the reach of exact sampling to larger circuits, enabling validation of quantum advantage and noise models.
method: The algorithm integrates tensor network contraction techniques with a Markov process, where a classical state evolves according to the local structure of the quantum circuit, allowing exact sampling from the output distribution.
result: They demonstrate exact sampling from ideal and noisy QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits, incorporating depolarizing and amplitude damping noise models, achieving a scale previously out of reach.
conclusion: This work significantly expands the scope of classical simulation in quantum algorithm research, providing a tool to test assumptions and conjectures at larger scales, and may inform the study of quantum advantage and noise effects.

title: Hoare Meets Heisenberg: A Lightweight Logic For Quantum Programs
authors: Aarthi Sundaram, Robert Rand, Kartik Singhal, Youngchan Cho, And Brad Lackey
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2172 (2026).

We show that Gottesman's (1998) semantics for Clifford circuits based on the Heisenberg representation gives rise to a lightweight Hoare-like logic for efficiently characterizing a common subset of quantum programs. Our applications include (i) certifying whether auxiliary qubits can be safely disposed of, (ii) determining if a system is separable across a given bipartition, (iii) checking the transversality of a gate with respect to a given stabilizer code, and (iv) computing post-measurement states for computational basis measurements. Further, this logic is extended to accommodate universal quantum computing by deriving Hoare triples for the [MATH]-gate, multiply-controlled unitaries such as the Toffoli gate, and some gate injection circuits that use associated magic states. A number of interesting results emerge from this logic, including a lower bound on the number of [MATH] gates necessary to perform a multiply-controlled [MATH] gate.

.
tldr: This paper introduces a lightweight Hoare-like logic for quantum programs based on Gottesman's Heisenberg representation, enabling efficient certification of properties like qubit disposal, separability, and gate transversality.
motivation: Verifying quantum programs is challenging; existing methods are often heavy. The authors aim to provide a lightweight logic for a common subset of quantum programs (Clifford circuits) and extend it to universal quantum computing.
method: They formalize a Hoare logic using Gottesman's semantics for Clifford circuits, deriving Hoare triples for Clifford operations and extending to non-Clifford gates like T-gates and Toffoli via magic states.
result: The logic enables efficient certification of auxiliary qubit disposal, bipartite separability, gate transversality, and post-measurement states. It also yields a lower bound on T-gates for multiply-controlled gates.
conclusion: The proposed logic provides a practical tool for reasoning about quantum programs, with potential applications in quantum error correction and circuit optimization.

title: Spin-based True Random Number Generation Enabled By Voltage-amplified Quantum Fluctuations
authors: Jie Zheng, Jiyong Kang, Zheng Zhu, Di Wu, Yuesheng Li, Dongxing Yu, Jiayong Wang, Hongxing Xu And Chenglong Jia
abstract: We investigate spin quantum-fluctuation effects that originate from the Heisenberg uncertainty principle during the dynamical cycle of disentanglement, entanglement, and re-disentanglement between itinerant electrons and localized magnetic moments mediated by the s–d exchange interaction. Beyond conventional deterministic spin-transfer torque, we analyze an intrinsic mechanism that transfers spin quantum fluctuations to a nanomagnet. By extending the Landau–Lifshitz–Gilbert equation to incorporate both quantum and thermal stochastic fields, we identify a temperature regime in which quantum fluctuations dominate the magnetization dynamics. We further show that voltage-controlled magnetic anisotropy exponentially amplifies spin quantum fluctuations, enabling binary readout through magnetoresistance in magnetic tunnel junctions. These findings provide a microscopic framework for fluctuation-driven spin dynamics and outline a device-level pathway toward spin-based quantum true random number generation.
tldr: This paper proposes a device-level mechanism for spin-based true random number generation by exploiting voltage-amplified quantum fluctuations in magnetic tunnel junctions.
motivation: To provide a microscopic framework for fluctuation-driven spin dynamics and a practical pathway for quantum true random number generation, which is relevant to hybrid quantum systems.
method: The authors extend the Landau–Lifshitz–Gilbert equation to include quantum and thermal stochastic fields, and analyze the effect of voltage-controlled magnetic anisotropy on spin quantum fluctuations.
result: They identify a temperature regime where quantum fluctuations dominate, and show that voltage-controlled magnetic anisotropy exponentially amplifies these fluctuations, enabling binary readout via magnetoresistance.
conclusion: The findings offer a device-level approach to spin-based quantum random number generation, contributing to hybrid quantum systems and quantum information processing.

title: Sparse Identification Of Quantum Hamiltonian Dynamics Via Quantum Circuit Learning
authors: Yusei Tateyama And Yuzuru Kato
abstract: Sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics (SINDy) is a data-driven framework for estimating classical nonlinear dynamical systems from time-series data. In this approach, system dynamics is represented as a linear combination of a predefined set of basis functions, and the corresponding coefficients are sparsely estimated from observed time-series data. In this study, we propose sparse identification of quantum Hamiltonian dynamics (SIQHDy), a SINDy-inspired quantum circuit learning framework for estimating quantum Hamiltonian dynamics from time-series data of quantum measurement outcomes. In SIQHDy, the unitary evolution of a quantum Hamiltonian system is expressed as a product of basis quantum circuits, and the corresponding circuit parameters are estimated through sparsity-promoting optimization. We numerically demonstrate that SIQHDy accurately reconstructs the dynamics of single-, three-, and five-spin systems, and exhibits robustness to measurement noise in the three-spin case. Furthermore, we propose an extension of SIQHDy for scenarios with limited accessible observables and evaluate its performance in identifying three-spin systems and in network-structure identification for five-spin systems.
tldr: This paper proposes a quantum circuit learning framework inspired by SINDy to sparsely identify quantum Hamiltonian dynamics from measurement time-series data.
motivation: Estimating quantum Hamiltonian dynamics from data is crucial for characterizing quantum systems, but existing methods may require many measurements or lack interpretability. The authors aim to adapt the classical SINDy approach to quantum systems using quantum circuits.
method: The method, SIQHDy, represents the unitary evolution as a product of basis quantum circuits and estimates circuit parameters via sparsity-promoting optimization. It also extends to scenarios with limited observables and network-structure identification.
result: Numerical demonstrations show accurate reconstruction of single-, three-, and five-spin systems, robustness to measurement noise in three-spin case, and successful network-structure identification for five-spin systems.
conclusion: SIQHDy provides a promising data-driven approach for identifying quantum Hamiltonian dynamics, with potential applications in quantum system characterization and quantum network inference.

title: Rotation-enhanced Photonic Spin Hall Effect In A Ring Bose–Einstein Condensate
authors: Leibo Deng, Muqaddar Abbas, Ghaisud Din, Hocine Bahlouli And Yong-Hong Ma
abstract: We show that rotation can strongly amplify the photonic spin Hall effect in a ring Bose–Einstein condensate. For an incident probe beam carrying orbital angular momentum (OAM), the spin-dependent transverse shift of the reflected light is weak in the non-rotating regime but becomes strongly enhanced under rotation because rotation lifts the degeneracy of the condensate mechanical modes via Bragg scattering. The resulting mode splitting produces large photonic spin Hall shifts at ultra-low optical power, with the enhancement increasing with both the condensate winding number and the probe OAM , while remaining weakly affected by atom–atom interactions. Our findings elucidate a rotation-governed mechanism underlying spin-dependent light transport in hybrid atom–optomechanical systems, thereby highlighting its potential for applications in high-precision rotational sensing.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that rotation can strongly enhance the photonic spin Hall effect in a ring Bose-Einstein condensate, enabling large spin-dependent shifts at ultra-low optical power.
motivation: The authors aim to understand and exploit rotation-governed mechanisms for spin-dependent light transport in hybrid atom-optomechanical systems, with potential applications in high-precision rotational sensing.
method: They theoretically analyze a ring BEC coupled to an optical cavity, considering Bragg scattering and mechanical mode degeneracy lifting due to rotation, and compute the photonic spin Hall shifts for incident probe beams carrying orbital angular momentum.
result: Rotation lifts the degeneracy of condensate mechanical modes, leading to large photonic spin Hall shifts that increase with condensate winding number and probe OAM, while being weakly affected by atom-atom interactions.
conclusion: The findings reveal a rotation-enhanced mechanism for spin-dependent light transport, highlighting the potential of ring BECs for high-precision rotational sensing and hybrid quantum systems.

title: Fate Of Entanglement In Open Quantum Spin Liquid: Time Evolution Of Its Genuine Multipartite Negativity Upon Sudden Coupling To A Dissipative Bosonic Environment
authors: Federico Garcia-Gaitan And Branislav K Nikolić
abstract: Many-body entanglement properties of quantum spin liquids (QSLs), persisting at arbitrarily long distances, have been intensely explored over the past two decades, but mostly for QSLs viewed as closed quantum systems. However, in experiments and potential quantum computing applications, candidate materials for this exotic phase of quantum matter will always interact with a dissipative environment, such as the one generated by bosonic quasiparticles in solids at finite temperature. Here we investigate both the stability and spatial distribution of entanglement for the Kitaev model of QSL, which is made open by its sudden coupling to an infinite bosonic bath of Caldeira–Leggett type and then time-evolved in both Markovian and non-Markovian regimes. From the time-dependent density matrix of QSL subregions, we extract genuine multipartite negativity (GMN), quantum Fisher information, spin–spin correlators, and the expectation value (EV) of the Wilson loop operator. In particular, time dependence of GMN offers the most penetrating insights: (i) in the Markovian regime, it remains nonzero only in hexagonal loopy subregions of QSL (as also discovered very recently for closed QSLs), eventually vanishing on the same timescale on which the EV of the Wilson loop operator vanishes; (ii) in the non-Markovian regime with pronounced memory effects, surprisingly, GMN remains nonzero up to much higher temperatures. In addition, the non-Markovian dynamics generates emergent interactions between spins, thereby opening avenues for tailoring properties of QSL via engineering of dissipation.
tldr: This paper studies the time evolution of genuine multipartite negativity in an open Kitaev quantum spin liquid coupled to a dissipative bosonic environment, revealing that non-Markovian dynamics can preserve entanglement at higher temperatures.
motivation: Quantum spin liquids are typically studied as closed systems, but real materials interact with dissipative environments. Understanding how entanglement in QSLs behaves under open system dynamics is crucial for quantum computing applications.
method: The authors model the Kitaev QSL suddenly coupled to a Caldeira-Leggett bosonic bath and time-evolve the system in both Markovian and non-Markovian regimes. They compute genuine multipartite negativity (GMN), quantum Fisher information, spin-spin correlators, and Wilson loop expectation values from the time-dependent density matrix of subregions.
result: In the Markovian regime, GMN remains nonzero only in hexagonal loopy subregions and vanishes on the same timescale as the Wilson loop expectation value. In the non-Markovian regime, GMN persists up to much higher temperatures, and emergent interactions between spins are generated.
conclusion: The findings suggest that engineering dissipation can tailor QSL properties, and non-Markovian effects can enhance entanglement stability, which is relevant for quantum information processing in open systems.

title: Temporal Coupled-Mode Theory For Quantum-Confined Stark Tuning Of Intersubband-Polaritonic Metasurfaces
authors: Inyong Hwang
abstract: ArXiv:2608.11538v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electrical tuning of intersubband-polaritonic metasurfaces requires a field-consistent connection between quantum-confined Stark effect (QCSE) modified transitions and measurable optical scattering. We derive a two-oscillator, one-port temporal coupled-mode theory (TCMT) and reduce the complex far-field reflection spectra of a metal-backed InGaAs/InAlAs metasurface over 21 electric fields. Self-consistent Schrodinger-Poisson calculations fix the intersubband energy and oscillator strength, while one zero-field complex calibration fixes the shared photonic parameters and a global phase-delay baseline; only the effective coupling remains field dependent. One hundred randomized initializations converge to the same zero-field parameter set. A reflectance-only control fits the intensity more closely but gives shifted modal parameters and a complex-amplitude error more than twice as large, establishing why the phase-resolved far field is required to identify the modal parameters and off-axis reflection-zero topology. The constrained model gives complex-amplitude RMSE values from 0.0256 to 0.0275 and separates the internal polariton poles from the external reflection zeros. The QCSE drives the two branch-associated zeros through the real-energy axis in opposite directions, producing branch-selective critical-coupling transitions within the same field intervals as the direct full-wave real-axis-zero cross-check. The resulting framework converts bias-resolved far-field spectra into an identifiable TCMT description without requiring a near-field observable.
tldr: This paper develops a temporal coupled-mode theory to model quantum-confined Stark tuning of intersubband-polaritonic metasurfaces, enabling extraction of modal parameters from far-field reflectance spectra.
motivation: Electrical tuning of intersubband-polaritonic metasurfaces requires a field-consistent connection between QCSE-modified transitions and measurable optical scattering, which is currently lacking.
method: The authors derive a two-oscillator, one-port TCMT and fit it to complex far-field reflection spectra of a metal-backed InGaAs/InAlAs metasurface over 21 electric fields, using self-consistent Schrödinger-Poisson calculations for intersubband energies and oscillator strengths, with only the effective coupling field-dependent.
result: The constrained model achieves complex-amplitude RMSE values from 0.0256 to 0.0275, separates internal polariton poles from external reflection zeros, and reveals branch-selective critical-coupling transitions driven by QCSE.
conclusion: The framework converts bias-resolved far-field spectra into an identifiable TCMT description without near-field observables, providing a practical tool for designing tunable metasurface devices.

title: Aggregation-engineered Loss-tolerant Strong Coupling In Metallic Microcavities
authors: Andrea Betti, Eleonora Cara, Giulia Serrano, Lorenzo Poggini, Alessia Valzelli, Natascia de Leo, Paolo Bartolini, Andrea Taschin, Renato Torre, Alice Boschetti
abstract: ArXiv:2608.11778v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Room-temperature strong coupling in organic microcavities is usually achieved by combining high-quality optical resonators with highly ordered excitonic media, a requirement that limits scalability and processing flexibility. Here we show that this constraint can be relaxed by using molecular aggregation as a design parameter rather than treating it as a parasitic effect. We realize solution-processed Rhodamine 6G-poly(vinyl alcohol) films embedded in low-quality-factor silver Fabry-Perot microcavities and demonstrate clear angle-resolved anticrossing with coupling energies up to 324 meV despite the large optical losses of the metallic mirrors. A two-exciton coupled-oscillator model shows that the relative weight of these species controls the collective coupling strength and can be tuned through dye loading and spin-coating conditions. In contrast, angle-resolved photoluminescence is dominated by a broad, red-shifted lower-polariton emission, consistent with relaxation through excimer-like states formed in densely packed molecular domains. These results identify molecular aggregation as a practical design lever for loss-tolerant strong coupling in wet-processed metallic cavities and suggest that ground-state aggregates and excited-state excimer-like species play distinct roles in polariton formation and emission.
tldr: This paper demonstrates loss-tolerant strong coupling in metallic microcavities by using molecular aggregation as a design parameter, achieving coupling energies up to 324 meV.
motivation: Room-temperature strong coupling in organic microcavities typically requires high-quality resonators and ordered excitonic media, limiting scalability. The authors aim to relax this constraint by exploiting molecular aggregation.
method: They fabricate solution-processed Rhodamine 6G-poly(vinyl alcohol) films in low-quality-factor silver Fabry-Perot microcavities and perform angle-resolved reflectivity and photoluminescence measurements, supported by a two-exciton coupled-oscillator model.
result: Clear anticrossing with coupling energies up to 324 meV is observed despite metallic losses, and the coupling strength is tunable via dye loading and spin-coating. Photoluminescence is dominated by red-shifted lower-polariton emission from excimer-like states.
conclusion: Molecular aggregation serves as a practical design lever for loss-tolerant strong coupling in wet-processed metallic cavities, with distinct roles for ground-state aggregates and excited-state excimers.

title: Exact Dynamical Structure Factor Of One-Dimensional Hard Rods And Its Universal Random Matrix Behavior
authors: Oleksandr Gamayun And Miłosz Panfil
abstract:

title: Exact Quantum Many-Body Scars In 2d Quantum Gauge Models
authors: Yuan Miao, Linhao Li, Hosho Katsura, And Masahito Yamazaki
abstract:
